newsitem.title: INDIA: Australia, India look past nuclear test ban split.
newsitem.headline: Australia, India look past nuclear test ban split.

text.p: Australia and India have buried deep differences over a global nuclear test ban treaty and can now join in pushing the nuclear powers to disarm, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Wednesday.
Downer told reporters in the Indian capital that the two nations had agreed their widely divergent stands on the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) should not affect expanding bilateral ties.

Last month Australia, skirting stymied arms talks in Geneva, shepherded the CTBT resolution which won overwhelming approval at the United Nations. India had blocked approval of the treaty at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, and refused to sign Australia's resolution.
Downer said New Delhi and Canberra had agreed that their differences over the CTBT would not be allowed to disrupt ties.

"It hasn't been a cause of tension in our bilateral relations at all," he told a news conference during a visit coinciding with the launch of a three-month festival highlighting Australian trade, science, sport and art.

The visiting Australian minister said that during talks on Tuesday with Indian officials it was clear the two countries could coordinate future disarmament steps as they both favoured eventual elimination of nuclear weapons.
"There is great scope for cooperation between Australia and India on nuclear disarmament issues," Downer said.

He said India and Australia had discussed the recommendations of a recent report by the independent, 17-member Canberra Commission, which called for "immediate and determined efforts" to eliminate nuclear weapons.
Downer said Delhi and Canberra could determine if they agreed "on a total road map for how we move towards the ultimate objective of the elimination of nuclear weapons".

John Dauth, first assistant secretary in the Australian Foreign Ministry, told Reuters that Australia and India could coordinate a position in favour of a treaty to halt production of bomb-making fissile material.

The Non-Aligned Movement, led by India, is demanding that negotiations to halt production of fissile material -- plutonium and highly-enriched uranium -- be linked to an agreement to launch fresh talks in Geneva next year on nuclear disarmament.
Last month Australia, Canada and New Zealand broke ranks somewhat with Western allies, calling for the Conference on Disarmament to address wider nuclear disarmament issues.
The five declared nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France Russia and the United States -- have refused to make such a commitment, preferring a step-by-step approach to disarmament.
Hailing stronger ties with India, Downer said he expected Australia's annual two-way trade with India, currently valued at about A$1.7 billion ($1.3 billion), to double in four years.
Australia's direct investment in India, currently valued at about A$600 million ($475 million), is likely to double in three to four years, he said.
Australia's High Commissioner (ambassador) to India, Darren Gribble, said his country was particularly interested in India's telecommunications, mining, insurance and agribusiness sectors.
Downer lamented Australia's failure on Monday to win a U.N. Security Council seat after two years of campaigning.
However, he noted India fell even farther short of its goal when Japan won 142 votes for the Asian non-permanent seat compared to India's 40. Australia gained 91 votes. (A$1 = $0.79)
